questions.concept: Why viruses sit outside the tree
questions.question: Why are viruses considered neither fully living nor fully non-living?
questions.solution: Outside a host: crystalline, inert, no metabolism — non-living chemistry. Inside a host: they hijack the host's machinery to replicate and evolve — living behaviour. Viruses have no own metabolism or ribosomes, only genetic information plus a protein coat; they are obligate intracellular parasites occupying the boundary.

questions.question: Both bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes. What molecular features separate the two domains?
questions.solution: Cell wall chemistry: bacteria use peptidoglycan; archaea use pseudopeptidoglycan or protein S-layers. Membrane lipids: archaea use ETHER-linked branched chains (bacteria: ester-linked). Gene machinery: archaeal RNA polymerase and ribosomes resemble EUKARYOTES more than bacteria. Molecular biology split 'prokaryotes' into two domains.

questions.question: Why do Gram-positive bacteria stain purple and Gram-negative pink, and why does the difference matter clinically?
questions.solution: Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan retains the crystal-violet–iodine complex even after alcohol decolourisation — purple. Gram-negative: thin peptidoglycan plus an outer membrane loses the complex and takes the pink counterstain. The wall structure also controls antibiotic entry (penicillin targets peptidoglycan synthesis) — so the stain predicts drug susceptibility.

questions.question: Why does milk undergo pasteurisation (72 °C, 15 s) rather than full sterilisation?
questions.solution: Pasteurisation kills pathogens and spoilage organisms while preserving milk's flavour and nutrients — a partial heat treatment targeting the dangerous species. Full sterilisation (high pressure steam) would destroy taste and vitamins. The trade-off: safety + quality vs absolute microbial zero.

questions.question: Why would a world without microbes be buried in organic matter within years?
questions.solution: Microbes (bacteria, fungi) are the biosphere's recyclers: they secrete enzymes that break cellulose, lignin and proteins into CO₂, water and minerals, returning them to soil and air. Plants could not access nutrients locked in dead matter; carbon and nitrogen cycles would halt. Decomposition is an ecosystem service only microbes perform at scale.

questions.concept: Why bacteria are grown in colonies
questions.question: Microbiologists streak plates to obtain isolated colonies rather than growing a single lawn. Why does an isolated colony matter?
questions.solution: A colony arising from one cell is a genetically uniform population — a clone — so its properties can be attributed to a single genotype and pure culture can be maintained. A lawn is a mixture, so any result is uninterpretable. Isolation is what makes a microbiological result reproducible.

questions.question: Viruses contain genetic material like cells but cannot reproduce alone. Why is a host strictly required?
questions.solution: A virus carries no ribosomes, no ATP-generating machinery and no metabolic enzymes — it has the instructions but none of the factory. It must enter a host cell and hijack that cell's replication and translation apparatus to make more virions. Absolute intracellular dependence is what separates viruses from organisms; they are obligate parasites at the machinery level.

questions.question: Penicillin kills bacteria but does nothing against flu. Why is antibacterial therapy inert against viruses?
questions.solution: Penicillin targets peptidoglycan cell-wall synthesis and other antibiotics hit bacterial ribosomes — structures viruses do not possess. Since viruses use host ribosomes and have no walls or bacterial metabolism, there is no target to hit. Selective toxicity requires a target the pathogen has and the patient lacks; viruses offer almost none, which is why antivirals are rarer and harder.
